opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few reasons, and some of them are practical while others are more philosophical.

On the practical side, the current recipe of scaling up data and compute has been remarkably successful, and I don't want to downplay that. But it's also becoming clear that we're approaching some limits. High-quality human-written text on the internet is finite, and the cost of training ever-larger models is enormous, not just financially but environmentally. That concentrates the ability to do cutting-edge AI research in a very small number of companies, and as an academic, I worry about that. If the only way to make progress is to have tens of thousands of GPUs, then most of the research community, and most of the world, gets shut out of shaping the technology.

But the more interesting reason for me is scientific. Humans don't learn this way. A child doesn't need to read trillions of words to understand that if you drop a glass it might break, or that people get upset when you take their things. We acquire an enormous amount of commonsense knowledge about the physical and social world from relatively little experience. So there's clearly something about how we learn: the abstractions we form, the way we generalize, the way we reason about cause and effect, that current models aren't capturing just by brute-force pattern matching over massive data.

And I think that gap shows up in the failure modes. These models can be astonishingly good at very hard tasks and then fail at something trivially easy for a person, because they've learned surface correlations rather than a robust understanding. So for me, looking for data-efficient learning isn't only about saving resources. It's a way of asking what intelligence actually is, and whether we can build systems that learn more the way humans do, with stronger generalization, more transparency, and frankly more alignment with human values and norms.

There's also a democratization angle that I care about a lot: smaller, more efficient models that are carefully trained on better data, whether that's distilled knowledge, curated or synthetic data, or more structured forms of commonsense, can sometimes rival much larger models on specific capabilities. That suggests that scale isn't the only lever, and that there's a lot of room for creativity and for ideas, not just resources, to drive progress.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling data and compute has been successful and discusses its limits, but it does not state that reliance on data is effectively the only currently known way to teach AI human knowledge and intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a couple of reasons, and they're kind of intertwined. The first one is just practical. If you look at where we are right now, the recipe for making progress has largely been scale: more data, more compute, bigger models. And that has worked remarkably well, I'm not going to deny that. But it also means that the frontier of AI research is increasingly concentrated in a very small number of organizations that can afford it. If you're in academia, or at a smaller lab, or frankly anywhere in the world that doesn't have access to tens of thousands of GPUs, you're kind of locked out of asking certain questions. So part of my motivation is, I want there to be a path forward that doesn't require brute force. I want to see what we can learn about intelligence when we can't just throw more data at the problem.

The second reason is more scientific, and honestly it's the one I find more exciting. Humans are incredibly data efficient learners. A child doesn't read the entire internet in order to learn language, or to learn that if you push a glass off the table it's going to fall and break. They see a handful of examples, and they generalize, and they build this rich model of the world that they can reason with. And current models, as impressive as they are, learn in a fundamentally different way. They consume orders of magnitude more text than any human could ever read, and yet they still make these strange, brittle mistakes on commonsense reasoning that a five-year-old wouldn't make. To me that gap is a signal. It's telling us that scale alone is not giving us the whole story about intelligence. There's something about how humans acquire knowledge, how we abstract, how we compose things we've learned, that we haven't captured yet.

And then there's a third piece, which is about what the data actually is. A lot of what's in web-scale training data is noisy, it's biased, it's redundant, and in some cases it's just wrong. So the question isn't only "can we use less data," it's "can we be more deliberate about what the model learns from." Can we distill the right kind of knowledge, whether that's commonsense, or reasoning procedures, or norms, in a way that's targeted rather than just hoping it emerges from the statistics of the entire web? I think if we get better at that, we end up with models that are not only cheaper to train but also more interpretable and more controllable, because we actually understand what went into them.

So for me, data efficiency isn't really about saving money, although that's nice. It's about understanding intelligence well enough that we don't have to rely on brute force to produce it.

r001.rationale: The response says AI progress has largely relied on more data, compute, and bigger models, but it does not state that relying on data is the only currently known way to teach AI human knowledge and intelligence.

astra-6.text:
I think the amount of data that machines need to learn today is telling us that something is missing in how we teach them. Humans don’t need to read the entire internet to learn how to reason about everyday situations. We learn from relatively few examples, and we can apply what we’ve learned to situations we haven’t encountered before.

So the motivation isn’t just to reduce the cost of training, although that matters. It’s also to ask what would allow a machine to generalize better. Can it learn the underlying concepts, rather than needing to see every possible variation? Common sense is particularly interesting here, because so much of what we know about the world is never explicitly written down. More text alone may not be enough; we also need better ways for machines to learn from it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reducing data needs and improving learning from text, but does not say reliance on data is the only currently known way to teach AI human knowledge and intelligence.

sol-6.1.text: Well, humans learn so much from relatively little experience. We don’t have to read the entire internet to learn how to reason about everyday situations. So I’m interested in understanding what makes that possible, and what we’re missing in the way we teach machines today. More data can certainly help, but I don’t think scale alone answers the question of intelligence. Can machines learn underlying concepts and apply them to situations they haven’t seen before? Finding more data-efficient ways to learn is both a practical goal and a way to investigate that deeper question.

r001.rationale: The response says more data can help and questions how machines are taught today, but it does not state that reliance on data is effectively the only currently known way to teach AI human knowledge and intelligence.
